posts.text:
The White House Chef, Andre Rush, has been  working inside the White House kitchen for almost 20 years. He has served, four Presidents, Clinton, Bush, Obama, and Trump. When asked which President was the most challenging to cook for, he answered it was Trump, because, he doesn't keep regular hours or have meals on a regular schedule.
He said, “He’s a worker. He’s up all night." The kitchen was always, prepared. The meals were ready, but Trump wasn't there to eat. He was too busy working.
Rush shared that the other three ate on a regular schedule. The chef could never predict when Trump would walk into the kitchen. Trump's schedule wasn't organized around meals. It revolved around his dedication to America.
He said Trump was, “Always friendly. Always complimentary to the staff.” Not once, throughout all those years, has Trump made the kitchen workers feel unimportant. No rude remarks. No unreasonable demands. 
No treatment that crossed the line, the kind of behavior powerful people sometimes display when they believe nobody significant is watching.
“He does try to eat healthy. People don’t get to see that part. They just see what we want to show on social media.”
For years, the media showed you Trump eating McDonald's and Diet Coke. Every reference carefully chosen to make him appear careless.
Rush revealed that behind every carefully selected picture is a man who is genuinely trying to look after his health — while staying awake all night, missing breakfast, and carrying 330 million people on his shoulders. 
Four Presidents, one chef who concluded that
Trump was the hardest President to cook for, not because he was hard to deal with, but because he was rarely there to eat. He was constantly working. Trump was always carrying the responsibilities, and repeatedly putting America First, ahead of his own meals. When he did arrive, he treated the people serving him with courtesy and kindness.

posts.text:
You can look up what your child's doctor is paid by vaccine makers. It is public, and it is free.

I am a Midwife in Pennsylvania. Parents ask me how to find this. Here is how.

The database is called Open Payments. It is run by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The search page is https://t.co/A40vIurOyj

1. Go to that page.
2. Type your doctor's first and last name. Add the city and state if the name is common.
3. Open the matching profile. Check the city and the specialty so you have the right person.
4. Look at the totals by year. The search tool now shows January 2019 through December 2025.
5. Look at the companies that paid the most. Then open the payment list and look for names like Merck, Pfizer, GSK, Sanofi, and Moderna.
6. You can also search those company names on the same site and see who they paid.
7. Save or download the list if you want to keep it.

If you find an old ProPublica tool called Dollars for Docs, skip it. It was last updated in 2019.

What you will see are meals, travel, consulting fees, speaking fees, education, gifts, research payments, and, for physicians, ownership or investment interests.

This covers doctors. Since the 2021 payment year it also covers physician assistants, nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists, nurse anesthetists, anesthesiologist assistants, and certified nurse- midwives. A traditional Midwife will usually not appear unless she is also a certified nurse- midwife.

The newest year on the site is 2025. Payments from 2026 are not public yet.

Very small payments do not always have to be reported. For 2025, a payment under $13.46 from one company can be left off, unless that company's payments to that provider added up to more than $134.54 for the year.

If your doctor is not in the database, it may mean there were no reportable payments, or the name is spelled differently. Try again with fewer letters, or add the city.

A listed payment is not proof of wrongdoing. CMS itself says a reported payment "does not necessarily mean" the relationship is improper. Research payments can look huge and often go to a hospital or a study, with the doctor listed as an investigator.

The totals are still large. For 2025 alone, CMS published $14.67 billion in payments and ownership interests, including $3.92 billion in general payments and $9.50 billion in research payments.

Here is what this database will NEVER show you.

It does not show what a practice makes when it buys vaccines and bills the insurance company.

It also does not show insurer quality bonuses. Some health plans pay extra when a practice hits childhood immunization targets, called Combo 10. One 2026 Health Net program in California pays $2,500 for each eligible Marketplace child when that gap is closed. That is one insurer's program, not a Pennsylvania rule. But it is the kind of money Open Payments will not list.

I believe you have a right to KNOW. I believe informed consent is not real if the money stays hidden. This is about transparency- not about telling you which shot to accept or refuse.

Ask your doctor, calmly, what they receive and why. You are allowed to have that conversation.

If you want to support this work, please consider buying me a coffee.

posts.text:
In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 Iran may have discovered something FAR MORE VALUABLE than a nuclear weapon: leverage over the world's OIL SUPPLY.

Brandon Weichert spoke with Quincy Institute board member Amir Handjani about Trump's blockade, Iran's threats to challenge it, and why neither side seems eager to restart a full-scale war.

During their conversation, news broke that the Tonya Star, an Iranian vessel believed to be challenging the blockade, had turned around in the Strait of Hormuz.

That hardly looks like a country desperate to start another shooting war.

But Amir thinks the current standoff can't last forever.

Iran needs to export its oil. And if the blockade continues into 2027, Tehran may decide escalation is worth the risk.

The Gulf states have their own reasons to oppose another American offensive.

Amir made a particularly interesting point: U.S. military bases were supposed to protect countries like Qatar and the UAE. Instead, he argues, those bases helped turn them into Iranian targets.

And he believes Gulf governments are beginning to reconsider whether American military protection is worth the exposure.

His longer-term prediction is even more consequential.

Iran could emerge from this war with a permanent role in managing traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, potentially alongside Oman.

Not because Washington wants that outcome, but because Tehran has demonstrated how much disruption it can cause.

Amir also doubts a Democratic Congress will actually cut off funding for the war, despite growing opposition to Trump's Iran policy.

So the immediate danger may not be a deliberate decision to launch another massive offensive.

It's that the blockade keeps squeezing Iran until Tehran decides it has more to gain by fighting than waiting.

And even if the war ends, Amir doesn't expect the old American security arrangement in the Gulf to simply return.
